**Synthetic Experiment:**
The purpose of the synthetic experiment was to show that MVCE properly penalized methods which diverged from the true generator, which is not possible on real data where we lack access to the true generator and are forced to use an approximation, as covered in section 7. We can further clarify this in the updated paper draft.

**Further references:**
We have several works already cited covering missing values from section 6, including notably Little & Rubin (2019) which summarizes the key missing value baselines, plus several recent works on missing values. We will look into the additional literature provided and cite any relevant works.

**Random vs Non-Random Patterns**
Our experiments on CelebA used non-random patterns of missingness (either top half or bottom half missing), while the multiclass experiments used random patterns (each region had a chance to be dropped). We can look into further experiments of non-random patterns on the multiclass setups, though due to the cost in running the diffusion model it would be infeasible to consider random patterns for CelebA without losing that baseline.

**Dataset Sizes:**
At test time as with ECE, having too few test samples will lead to issues in computing MVCE as too few samples in a bin makes consistency (an average of a binary label) never match confidence (a probability for each sample). We did not believe ablations to find the minimal amount of training data to train DMV to be interesting; instead we stuck to standard splits for our chosen datasets.

**Real Data:**
It is unclear what the reviewer means by "real data", as all our datasets other than synthetic are based on real data. Are you referring to datasets with "real" missingness as opposed to a simulated mutator?

**References**

Roderick JA Little and Donald B Rubin. Statistical analysis with missing data, volume 793. John
Wiley & Sons, 2019.

summary.value: Paper proposes a framework for missing value uncertainty of classification methods in the case of missing input values at inference time. This can be used in decision making to collect more information, if required. Computationally efficient estimator called direct missing value is derived to overcome computational challenges of Monte Carlo (MC) sampling, as well as missing value calibration error metric for evaluation and post-hoc calibration of the model. Proposed methodologies are evaluated and compared to a few baselines on synthetic and real data with promising results.

strengths.value:
To my knowledge, paper proposes novel approach to uncertainty quantification of missing input data on a test-time, more rarely studied compared to first-order uncertainty and the calibration of soft confidence, and could provide interesting addition and complementary information to uncertainty modelling in trustworthy ML and active decision making in critical application areas. The more specific contributions are 1) the formulation of the framework, 2) computational improvements against MC baseline with new estimator for missing value uncertainty, and 3) new error metric for this particular setting (inspired by expected calibration error (ECE) typically used to evaluate and estimate the output calibration). The empirical evaluations are done to support and justify the most of the claims.

Summary of strengths:
- Novel and interesting approach
- Computational improvements against baseline
- New metric and estimator proposed
- Experiments show some usefulness

weaknesses.value:
Although paper is generally sound and the most of the claims are supported by the empirical evaluations, there are some weaknesses related to experiments to better justify and support the findings and the significance of the work. First, there could be more versatile evaluation baselines and discussion of prior work of why particular simple baselines (e.g., imputation and missing robust models) are chosen and how would more advanced methods affect the evaluation. Second, analysis of proposed error metrics (MVCE) could be examined more detailed and its relation to other metrics in the literature. Third, masked image dataset are used in experiments, but it  is unclear how the proposed approach could perform in other modalities such as tabular data (with missing inputs) or data from medical and sensor network domains mentioned in the paper. Clarification for these could improve the quality and significance of the work (see also specific questions below).

Summary of Weaknesses
- Insufficient connection to prior work and utilised baselines in the discussion and experiments (i.e., why particular simple baselines are chosen)
- Limited analysis of proposed error metric (MVCE) against other metrics in the literature (and its properties/parameters)
- Limitations on evaluated datasets (e.g., missing of modalities such as real tabular data or those critical application domains mentioned in the paper)

We have updated the paper based on feedback received in reviews and discussion among our authors. This notably includes improvements to the prose which have been highlighted in blue in the main body of the paper to make them easier to identify, along with updates to results in both the main body and the appendix.

Results were notably switched from reporting consistency to reporting clean accuracy (accuracy with no missing values) and mutated accuracy (main test accuracy considering the mask), as we believe this is both more comparable to prior work and easier to interpret as a performance metric. We continue to use consistency on each bin as part of MVCE for reasons explained in the paper.

summary.value: This paper introduces a framework for Missing Value Uncertainty (MVU), which is the distribution of predictions induced by incomplete inputs. The authors formalize the problem by defining hard confidence: the probability that a prediction will not change after collecting the missing data. Thus, they propose a novel Direct Missing Value (DMV) to efficiently estimate the MVU distribution, bypassing the need for expensive Monte Carlo sampling. Furthermore, They introduce the Missing Value Calibration Error (MVCE), a new metric specifically designed to evaluate the calibration of hard confidence values, and a post-hoc calibration procedure to improve MVU estimation. They showcase their method and metric on synthetic and real-world datasets. Notwithstanding, the reviewers have identified several weaknesses of this paper. In particular, most of the claims are supported just by empirical evaluations, though there could be more versatile evaluation baselines and discussion of prior work. Furthermore, an analysis of proposed error metrics (MVCE) could be examined more detailed and its relation to other metrics in the literature. Moreover, it is unclear how the proposed approach could perform in other modalities. The reviewers have also indicated that the authors ignore critical aspects of missing data, including whether the data is missing at random and how much data is missing for a variable of interest in terms of its overall impact on outcomes. The reviewers have also indicated that the paper lacks sufficient detail to fully understand how the proposed method is implemented in practice. Furthermore, they indicate that the main assumption of the paper is restrictive, as real-world datasets with missing values often violate MAR. Finally, they also indicate that the authors seem to ignore a rich existing literature on active feature acquisition at test time. Overall, while the contribution is original and potentially has impact, the empirical validation and discussion of related work need significant improvement to justify acceptance.

summary.value:
The paper aims to provide a tool to estimate, for each sample, the probability that a decision based on a probabilistic classifier would change if more data were available. This can guide decision-makers on whether additional data collection is worthwhile. The targeted uncertainty is a form of epistemic uncertainty, but orthogonal to the usual notion: rather than uncertainty due to model suboptimality (reducible by more training data), it captures uncertainty due to unobserved variables (reducible by completing missing data).
The authors define **Missing Value Uncertainty (MVU)** as the distribution of a model’s probabilistic predictions when only a subset of features is observed — i.e., the variability in predictions induced by the distribution of missing values. They propose an efficient estimator, the **Direct Missing Value estimator (DMV)**, which bypasses sampling in potentially high-dimensional spaces or imputation. In practice, MVU is modeled using a Dirichlet distribution.

They also introduce the notions of **hard prediction** (majority vote) and **hard confidence** (the proportion of predictions agreeing with the majority), along with a new evaluation metric, the **Missing Value Calibration Error (MVCE)**, which mirrors Expected Calibration Error (ECE) but measures how well hard confidence reflects the empirical probability of prediction changes between partial and complete data. A recalibration method tailored to this setting is also proposed.

Experiments on synthetic and image-based datasets compare DMV to sampling (via diffusion) and imputation baselines in terms of MVCE, as well as the recalibration quality.

strengths.value:
**Novelty**: The authors introduce and formalize a new class of uncertainty quantification problems, addressing a question of clear practical relevance: whether one should collect additional data before making a decision. To my knowledge, no prior work has explicitly or rigorously formulated this problem, making this contribution useful and original.

**Clarity of formalization**: The underlying intuition is articulated very clearly, and the resulting problem formulation is precise and easy to follow.

**Efficient estimator**: The proposed estimator avoids the need for costly and difficult sampling of missing values given observed ones, offering a more elegant and practical solution for estimatingMVU.

weaknesses.value:
**Clarity of the practical aspects** :  The paper lacks sufficient detail to fully understand how the proposed method is implemented in practice. This is an important weakness, as it prevents a thorough evaluation of the approach’s validity and effectiveness. Specific issues are detailed in the questions section.

**Evaluation of the MVU estimator**: Estimating MVU is a very challenging task—typically harder than learning the optimal probabilistic prediction under arbitrary missingness—because it requires estimating the full predictive distribution rather than just the conditional expectation. I am therefore wondering how well DMV can approximate this distribution, and the current experiments do not convince me that it is indeed a good estimator.

For example, Table 2 shows that DMV achieves an MVCE roughly comparable to a diffusion-based sampling baseline using only 3 samples (in 2 out of 3 tasks). It is questionable whether 3 samples suffice to accurately approximate the MVU distribution, which raises concerns about whether DMV captures the distribution’s quality well enough. 

Validating DMV on a controlled synthetic setting (e.g., a multivariate Gaussian) would allow comparison against a ground-truth baseline, exploring how performance varies with dimensionality, sample size, and other factors. It would also allow to compare to a sampling baseline in a controlled setting where many samples can be drawn, and see what the estimation quality/computational tradeoffs are more clearly.


**Assumptions limiting practical applicability**

- **MAR assumption**: According to line 363, the proposed method is valid only under the MAR (missing at random) assumption. While common, this assumption is restrictive, as real-world datasets with missing values often violate MAR. The authors should clarify precisely where and why this assumption is required in their method.

- **Complete training data**: The method requires complete training data, with missing values handled only at inference time. This limits its applicability in settings where comlpete training data is available.


**Conclusion** - I think the theoretical and formalization contribution is very interesting and impactful. Yet the experiments (and lack of details thereof) do not convince me that the proposed estimator is effective (and in which scenarios).

comment.value:
Refer also to the general reviewer response, which discusses MVU in practice, experiment modality, and clarifies our paper's scope.

**EDDI:**
EDDI (Ma et al., 2019) is already cited in our paper. Their work does not consider the classification task, at best giving us another option for inpainting. Other works suggest their method is expensive at high feature count, so we do not believe the method will be notably faster than Copaint diffusion.

**GSM:**
We were not aware of the work on GSM by Li et al. (2021), and agree it is related to our task, though their problem is different. Our goal is identifying simply whether collecting missing features may change the prediction, while they ask which feature is the best to collect (though also considering the prediction unlike EDDI). They have a terminating condition on when to stop collecting features which answers a similar question to us, though they directly use $p(y|x_o)$ to accomplish the goal. This is equivalent to $\phi$ in our notation, making their work match up to the soft-confidence approach which does not directly consider the variance of missing values. We will look into their work as an additional baseline for our experiments.

**Flexibility:**
Our work simply answers the question of whether you need to collect missing features and does not consider which features to collect after that determination. Per our general reviewer response, we believe that our title was misinterpreted and proposed a reworked title that is more precise along with an update to the relevant introduction paragraphs. Thus, while I agree that partially revealing features is a reasonable extension, I believe it is out of scope of our current work. Some existing works (such as the ones you highlighted) could be used to answer that part of the question.

**Synthetic Methods:**
The synthetic methods were based off 5 different multivariate gaussian generators: the ground truth that generated the dataset, and several that mutated the correlation between the variables or the covariance as described in the table. 100 samples of the generator was used in the Monte Carlo approach. Additionally, we used a simple zero imputation (which is also the generator mean in this case) and one of the baselines from section 4.1 for estimating variance as a non-generator baseline. We will clarify this in an updated paper draft.

Below are responses to concerns raised by multiple reviewers, collected to simplify discussion. We additionally will reply individually to each reviewer to answer specific questions they had.

We are working on an updated draft of the paper which includes the clarifications and improvements mentioned in other replies. After posting the updated draft, we will determine which of the proposed experiments are feasible to complete within the author/reviewer discussion period.

**Misleading Title:**
Based on reviewer comments, we found our main paper question was phrased in a misleading way. We asked whether it is worth it to collect missing values, but our goal was to quantify whether collecting missing values may change the prediction. Assuming the prediction might change, we do not currently consider the cost of collecting those values.
Based on this, we will update the title of the work to "Missing Value Uncertainty: Will collecting missing values change the prediction?" and make the appropriate changes to the introduction to match the question the rest of the paper answered.

**MVU in Practice:**
As far as using MVCE in practice, it is a performance metric so you cannot use it to make a decision without access to ground truth. MVU can be used through computing hard confidence, and then selecting a threshold for when to accept the prediction. As stated on line 48, you can interpret hard confidence as "the probability a prediction will not change if missing values are collected"; e.g. a threshold of 0.9 can be interpreted as "accept if there is a 90% chance the prediction will not change". We will include this threshold example in the paper.

**Type and Amount of Missingness**
Our work states that we considered just MAR for missing type, but we do not believe this is a limitation in our methods. We agree the experiments could be expanded to cover more types of missingness such as MNAR along with different amounts of missingness.
None of our imputation or generator approaches are trained considering a particular method of missingness, so at most the method of missingness for those baselines simply produce a new task via a different mutator. DMV training may benefit from choosing an appropriate type of missingness if you believe that is the type of missingness that will be present during evaluation; we will consider experiments where we do not know the mutator during training of DMV.

**Experiment Modality:**
I will also note our experiments do not require dropping continuous regions; while the individual sections dropped are continuous, the overall set of dropped features may not be connected.
We agree that additional modalities is worth exploring; we had previously considered tabular datasets as our work is not limited to images, though they ended up dropped in this version. We will look into restoring tabular dataset experiments, such as using the datasets from Li et al. (2021) mentioned by reviewer nLXu (which notably includes a medical tabular dataset).

**References**

Li Y et al. Active Feature Acquisition with Generative Surrogate Models. ICML. 2021.

Refer also to the general reviewer response regarding the type of missingness and MVU in practice.

**Evaluating MVU:**
It is a fair criticism that DMV only performed as well as the 3 sample diffusion approach on the Smiling CelebA feature, though on the other two features it was able to perform as as well as the 30 sample approach (after calibration in the case of Blond Hair). Based on this, we believe further training or hyperparameter tuning during the DMV training could further improve the performance of DMV on Smiling.
The suggestion to compare against a controlled synthetic setting is a fair suggestion, we will look into an experiment validating DMV on synthetic data.

**Complete training data:**
While it is true that our work requires complete training data, DMV training is for the most part standard neutral network training with a modified loss function. Assuming you have an approach to train the "clean classifier" (that is, the classifier that outputs $\phi$ values), you should be able to use the same approach for DMV, simply applying additional mutations to construct the pairs of "clean" prediction and masked predictions needed for equation 9.

**Dirichlet distribution to hard confidence:**
Since the equations for $y_hard$ and $c_hard$ require performing expectations over expectations over $p(\phi)$, we used Monte Carlo sampling with 1000 samples to estimate those values. Since the size of $\alpha$ is the same as the number of classes, this distribution is efficient to sample from even for methods where computing the distribution may be inefficient. We choose 1000 as we did not see a notable difference in results upon further increasing it to 10000 in earlier tests, though too few samples would give you a poor estimate. We will update section 7 with the relevant information.

**Imputation Baseline:**
The imputation baseline simply requires constructing a tensor same size as the input. For mean imputation, this was constructed by taking the mean of all training images in the dataset. Any features that were missing at runtime were replaced with the feature from the mean tensor. We will include this information in the appendix.

**Synthetic Experiment:**
The synthetic experiment mean imputation baseline used the max variance approach described in section 4.1. The generator approaches all used Monte Carlo with 100 samples. We will add this information to section 7.

**DMV Architecture:**
We described the architecture of the DMV method in the appendix on line 790, which is a slightly modified ResNet18 classifier. The input layer is modified to take a 4th image channel representing the mask (boolean indicating for each pixel whether it is missing), and the final activation function is swapped from a softmax to an exponential, we can include a summary of this information in section 7.
We trained DMV using the same training split as the standard classifier, which contained 26000 images for CelebA. Other datasets used 70\% of the training split, holding out the remaining 30\% for validation. We did not believe ablations to find the minimal amount of training data to train DMV to be interesting; instead we stuck to standard splits for our chosen datasets.

**MVCE Bins:**
As mentioned in the appendix on line 775, we used 10 bins for computing MVCE, all equal sized by evenly dividing the range from 0 to 100%. Practically, only the top 5 bins are used for CelebA as its a binary classification (hard confidence cannot go below 0.5), and the top 9 bins for the 10 class datasets (as hard confidence cannot go below 0.1).

**MAR Assumption:**
Our work does not say our method is only valid under MAR, line 363 simply says we only considered MAR in our work.
The MAR assumption is only relevant to our choice of mutator. At training time, this only affects DMV, while at testing time this mutator is used to evaluate all methods.
See our general comment on types of missingness for more discussion of this topic.

I believe you misunderstood what I wrote in my comment. We have two different mask setups at test time, CelebA uses a fixed mask and the randomized masks on multiclass, so we are not simply using MNAR as your comment suggests.

To be completely clear on the randomness of missing, the multiclass setups randomly drop regions in both training of DMV and during evaluation (see line 807 from the appendix), making it fully MAR. The CelebA experiment has a set of 4 masks that are randomly selected during training, but at evaluation time it uses a single fixed choice for each experiment (see line 845 in the appendix). I could see the argument for calling the evaluation of CelebA with the fixed mask "MNAR", but given the majority of our work uses MAR and our main paper reports averages of the different masks for CelebA, MNAR did not seem accurate.

Refer also to our general reviewer response comment on experiment modality.

**Baselines:**
Our goal with the evaluation baselines was to provide several representative methods rather than evaluate every method for handling missing values; unless the method also provides an equivalence to MVU it would still require using one of our variance baselines to compare it using MVCE to our DMV. Working on image data limited the applicability of many of the methods for handling missing values we cited, as they either did not scale to images or were expensive when scaled.

**Analysis of Metric:**
Since submitting this paper, we have been working on updated tables which include accuracy under missing values compared to accuracy on the clean test set for each experiment (replacing consistency which is less intuitive outside of MVCE). This matches up to what several prior works seemed to be using to evaluate the effectiveness of their missing value handling methods. We will include this metric in an updated draft of the paper, which we believe appropriately shows that while some baselines can get high accuracy, accuracy alone is insufficient to evaluate whether you computed a useful measure for MVU.
We do not believe there is another existing metric that directly can evaluate hard confidence; the closest we are aware of is ECE which was the basis for our metric and in our terms is evaluating soft confidence.

**Sensor Data:**
The StarCraft dataset images contains recordings of two players in a competitive strategy game; removing regions of the images approximates sensors in a battlefield scenario. See the general comment for further discussion on dataset modalities.

**MVCE Hyperparamters:**
The behavior of the bin size will mirror bins in ECE largely; too many bins risks having too few samples in a bin to ever have the bin consistency match the average bin confidence, while too few bins can easily collapse to just comparing average confidence to total consistency (which is not ideal as some samples should estimate less confidence).
Keeping the bin count consistent across experiments was simply to minimize variables as we believed 10 to be a good choice for all datasets, though we could consider experiments on varying the bin size in MVCE and how it impacts results.

**Computational Efficiency:**
We did not collect efficiency for other baselines as the times of non-diffusion methods on CelebA were all within a small margin of error of each other so did not believe they were notable for other datasets. None of our methods for estimating MVU scale beyond linear with the number of classes. The "Missing Robust" method I will note is a similar architecture to DMV, so the performance should be comparable. We can look into collecting these times for other datasets, though fairly obtaining the times requires minimizing variables which reduces the speed we can run the experiments (e.g. not running multiple methods at once in parallel).

summary.value: This study formalises Missing Value Uncertainty (MVU), which is the epistemic uncertainty introduced by not observing all input features for a given sample at test time. They then propose Direct Missing Value (DMV) as an efficient way to estimate the MVU and introduce the Missing Value Calibration Error (MVCE) as a new metric to quantify the added value of collecting currently missing values. The MVCE is evaluated in a synthetic data experiment, whereas the DMV is compared to a diffusion model on CelebA and two simple baselines on MNIST, CIFAR10, and StarcraftCIFAR10.

strengths.value: The paper is well written and introduces a novel notion of quantifying the value of information of missing data at test time based on probabilistic predictors and hard voting.

weaknesses.value:
**Novelty** : The authors seem to ignore a rich existing literature on active feature acquisition at test time such as Ma et al. (2019) or Li et al. (2021). These methods seem to address the same question posed by the authors: "Is it worth it to collect missing values (for this specific test sample)?" Existing methods need to be discussed in the paper and must be included as baselines in the experiments (or a strong case must be made why they in fact should not be included as baselines) to show the relativ merit of the proposed approach. 

Ma C et al. EDDI: Efficient Dynamic Discovery of High-Value Information with Partial VAE. ICML. 2019.
Li Y et al. Active Feature Acquisition with Generative Surrogate Models. ICML. 2021. 

**Flexibility**: In the current version, the introduced methods only dicuss an all-or-nothing setting in which either no additional information is collected (sticking with the initial $X_O$) or all missing values are obtained (resulting in $X$). However, it may often be interesting to collect only the most informative one or two additional values or to sequentially obtain values. 

**Experiments**: The included experiments are limited to dropping continuous regions of common image datasets. Following previous literature like EDDI, experiments with additional modalities like tabular data would be beneficial. The authors also don't discuss how their derived consistency or MVCE should be used in practice to make a decision to collect additional data, and what benefit the user would obtain by doing so.
